hook: The reformer who made Geneva a Protestant city and inspired churches worldwide.

pages.x: Jean Calvin was born in 1509 at Noyon, in northern France. His father had him study law, but in his twenties he had what he called a "sudden conversion" to the Protestant faith, and had to flee France when Protestants were hunted down.

At 26, in Basel, he published the Institutes of the Christian Religion, a clear and orderly account of Protestant belief. He revised it all his life, and it became one of the most influential books of the Reformation.

Passing through Geneva in 1536, he meant to stay a single night. The fiery preacher William Farel told him God would curse him if he left. Calvin stayed. The city threw him out two years later, then begged him to come back in 1541.

In Geneva he built a strict Protestant city: dancing, gambling and fancy clothes were banned, and elders watched over everyone's morals. Refugees came from all over Europe; the Scottish reformer John Knox called it "the most perfect school of Christ".
In 1553 Michael Servetus, a Spanish doctor who denied the Trinity, was arrested in Geneva. Calvin backed his trial, and Servetus was burned at the stake. It shocked many people even then.

In 1559 he founded the Geneva Academy, today the University of Geneva, to train ministers. They carried his teaching to France, the Netherlands and Scotland. When he died in 1564 he asked to be buried in an unmarked grave.

Calvin's teaching shaped the Reformed and Presbyterian churches, the Huguenots of France, the Dutch and the Puritans who settled New England. Some historians link the "Protestant work ethic" to his ideas.
pts: Wrote the Institutes of the Christian Religion
Inspired Reformed and Presbyterian churches worldwide
